cross_contact_notes: Found in most baked goods, sauces, and creamy dishes. Butter is often used in cooking even when not listed.
notes: Dairy is one of the FDA Big-9 major allergens. Lactose intolerance is different from a milk allergy — allergen concerns relate to milk proteins (casein, whey), not lactose.

cross_contact_notes: Eggs are used as binders, coatings, and emulsifiers in many dishes. Egg wash is commonly applied to pastries.
notes: FDA Big-9 allergen. Eggs are in many sauces, batters, and baked goods even when not prominently listed.

cross_contact_notes: Fish sauce and anchovies are hidden in many sauces, dressings, and condiments. Caesar dressing almost always contains anchovies.
notes: FDA Big-9 allergen. Fish sauce is a common hidden source in Asian cuisine. Worcestershire sauce contains anchovies.

cross_contact_notes: High cross-contact risk in restaurants that serve seafood broadly. Shrimp paste is used as a base flavoring in many Asian dishes.
notes: FDA Big-9 allergen. Shellfish allergy is separate from fish allergy — patients may be allergic to one and not the other.

common_dishes_containing: pad thai (peanut but cross-contact with tree nuts)
cross_contact_notes: Mole sauce traditionally contains ground almonds or other tree nuts. Pesto contains pine nuts. Many desserts contain almond flour or extracts.
notes: FDA Big-9 allergen. Coconut is classified as a tree nut by the FDA, though many nut-allergic individuals tolerate it. Pine nuts are seeds but classified as tree nuts for labeling. Mole is one of the most commonly missed hidden sources.

hidden_names: artificial tree nut flavor (may be peanut-derived)
cross_contact_notes: Peanuts and tree nuts are often processed in the same facilities, creating high cross-contact risk. Peanut is one of the most common and severe food allergens.
notes: FDA Big-9 allergen. Despite the name, peanuts are legumes, not tree nuts. Cross-contact with tree nuts is very common. Thai and other Asian cuisines make heavy use of peanuts.

common_dishes_containing: most asian stir fry dishes (soy sauce)
cross_contact_notes: Soy sauce almost always contains wheat. 'Gluten-free' claims on menus may not be certified — cross-contact risk in shared kitchens is significant.
notes: FDA Big-9 allergen. Distinct from celiac disease (autoimmune) but closely related for dietary restriction purposes. Soy sauce is a major hidden wheat source in Asian cuisine.

cross_contact_notes: Soy is pervasive in Asian cuisine and processed foods. Miso, teriyaki, and most Asian stir-fry sauces contain soy.
notes: FDA Big-9 allergen. Highly refined soy oil and soy lecithin are sometimes tolerated by soy-allergic individuals, but this varies.

cross_contact_notes: Sesame became an FDA Big-9 allergen in 2023. It is present in many Middle Eastern and Asian dishes. Tahini (sesame paste) is a core ingredient in hummus.
notes: Newest FDA Big-9 allergen (added January 2023). Sesame is particularly prevalent in Middle Eastern, Mediterranean, and Asian cuisines.

fda_category: major allergen in Canada/EU (not FDA Big-9)
cross_contact_notes: Curry powder almost always contains mustard seed. Important allergen in EU/Canada even if not FDA Big-9.
notes: Not an FDA Big-9 allergen but a major allergen in Canada and EU. Common in condiments, dressings, and Indian/curry dishes.

common_dishes_containing: dried fruit in salads or desserts
cross_contact_notes: Shrimp is commonly treated with sulfites for preservation. Wine-based cooking introduces sulfites.
notes: Not a protein allergen but causes reactions in sulfite-sensitive individuals, particularly those with asthma.

description: Excludes all animal products: meat, poultry, fish, seafood, dairy, eggs, honey, gelatin, and all other animal-derived ingredients.
hidden_violators: chicken stock
beef broth
fish stock
bone broth
fish sauce
worcestershire sauce
anchovy paste
shrimp paste
gelatin (in desserts, marshmallows, panna cotta, jello)
rennet (in parmesan, many hard cheeses)
casein (in some non-dairy creamers)
carmine / cochineal / E120 (red food dye derived from insects)
isinglass (used to clarify some wines and beers)
caesar dressing (contains anchovies and egg)
lard (in some refried beans, pastry, tamales)
L-cysteine (dough conditioner sometimes animal-derived)
commonly_violated_dishes: most soups and broths (made with chicken or beef stock)
miso soup (dashi broth often contains fish)
most breads and baked goods (butter, eggs, milk)
notes: Vegan excludes all animal-derived ingredients including less obvious ones like gelatin, rennet, carmine, and isinglass. Stock and broth are the most common hidden violations in restaurant cooking — almost all soups, sauces, and risottos are made with animal stock unless explicitly specified. Caesar dressing is almost never vegan.

description: Excludes meat, poultry, fish, and seafood. Dairy and eggs are permitted.
hidden_violators: chicken stock or broth (in soups, risotto, sauces)
beef stock or broth (in french onion soup, stews, gravies)
fish stock or dashi (in miso soup, asian broths)
fish sauce (in pad thai, vietnamese, thai dishes)
worcestershire sauce (contains anchovies)
caesar dressing (contains anchovies)
gelatin (in panna cotta, jello, some marshmallows, some candies)
rennet (animal-derived rennet in parmesan, pecorino, and most aged cheeses)
lard (in some tamales, refried beans, pie crusts, pastries)
anchovy paste (in some pasta sauces, pizza toppings)
carmine / cochineal / E120 (red food dye from insects)
commonly_violated_dishes: most restaurant soups (chicken or beef stock base)
most pasta sauces at restaurants (may use chicken stock)
kimchi (sometimes contains fish sauce or shrimp paste)
notes: Vegetarian allows dairy and eggs but excludes all meat, poultry, and seafood. The most common hidden violations are animal-based stocks (chicken, beef, fish) used as the base for soups, sauces, and grains. Fish sauce and Worcestershire sauce (contains anchovies) are frequent hidden violations in Asian and international dishes. Parmesan and many aged cheeses use animal rennet — strictly vegetarian diners often avoid these.

description: Excludes wheat, barley, rye, and their derivatives. Suitable for celiac disease and gluten intolerance.
hidden_violators: soy sauce (almost all brands contain wheat — use tamari for gluten-free)
malt and malt vinegar (barley-derived)
beer and beer batter (barley-based)
modified food starch (may be wheat-derived)
hydrolyzed vegetable protein (may contain wheat)
roux-based sauces and gravies (flour + butter thickener)
battered and fried foods (flour or breadcrumb coating)
seitan (pure gluten — often in vegetarian dishes)
imitation crab / surimi (often contains wheat starch)
some oats (cross-contact with wheat during processing)
most sauces thickened with flour
dressings and marinades containing soy sauce
teriyaki, hoisin, oyster sauce (most brands contain wheat)
licorice and some candies
commonly_violated_dishes: fried foods with batter (tempura, fish and chips, onion rings)
most baked goods (bread, muffins, cakes, cookies, pastries)
pad thai (soy sauce, sometimes flour noodles)
notes: Gluten is found in wheat, barley, rye, and cross-contaminated oats. Soy sauce is the most common hidden gluten source in restaurant cooking — nearly all soy sauce brands contain wheat. Roux (butter + flour) is the base for many sauces and gravies. Cross-contact in shared fryers and kitchens is a serious concern for celiac patients. 'Gluten-free' on a menu does not guarantee a certified gluten-free preparation.

description: Excludes all milk and dairy products including milk, cheese, butter, cream, yogurt, and their derivatives.
hidden_violators: casein and caseinate (milk protein used in some non-dairy products and processed foods)
whey and whey protein (dairy byproduct in protein bars, breads, sauces)
ghee (clarified butter — still contains milk proteins)
cream sauces (bechamel, mornay, alfredo, veloute)
au gratin dishes (cream + cheese topping)
most baked goods (butter, milk, or cream)
milk chocolate and white chocolate
caramel sauce (most recipes use butter and cream)
ranch dressing and most creamy dressings
caesar dressing (parmesan)
pesto (parmesan)
mashed potatoes (butter and cream)
most Indian curries (cream, ghee, paneer, yogurt marinade)
naan bread (yogurt or butter)
some margarines (may contain casein or whey)
non-dairy creamer (many brands contain casein)
lactose-free milk (still contains milk proteins — not dairy-free)
commonly_violated_dishes: most baked goods (bread, muffins, cookies, cakes, pastries)
most desserts (ice cream, custard, creme brulee, cheesecake, tiramisu)
most Indian dishes (butter chicken, paneer dishes, korma, tikka masala)
creamy dressings (ranch, blue cheese, caesar, creamy italian)
notes: Dairy-free is distinct from lactose-free — dairy-free excludes all milk proteins (casein, whey) while lactose-free products still contain milk. Ghee (clarified butter) retains milk proteins and is not dairy-free despite being lactose-reduced. Cream sauces (alfredo, bechamel) and butter are the most common hidden dairy sources in restaurant cooking. Many baked goods contain butter even when not listed prominently. Parmesan appears in many dishes including pesto, caesar dressing, and risotto.
